notes.meaning: Jeremiah writes a letter from Jerusalem to the Jewish elders, priests, prophets, and people living in Babylon. This happened after King Jeconiah, his mother, and many skilled craftsmen had been carried away as captives. Jeremiah sent the letter through two royal messengers whom King Zedekiah dispatched to King Nebuchadnezzar. God made sure His scattered people received His true guidance even when they were far away from home.

God speaks using His royal title, the Lord of Hosts, showing that He commands all the armies of heaven and earth. He reminds the people that He Himself sent them into exile, using the Babylonians to carry out His purpose. The captives were not merely victims of world politics, but were under God's own fatherly correction. Recognizing God's hand in our hardships helps us accept them with patience.

God tells the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and eat the food they grow. They are also told to marry, have children, and help their children marry so their families will multiply instead of shrink. This proved their time in Babylon would not be short, so they needed to settle down rather than live out of suitcases. God wanted to preserve Abraham's family and keep them strong even during their years of discipline.

The Lord commands the exiles to seek the peace and prosperity of the pagan city where they live. They are told to pray to God on Babylon's behalf, because if the city flourishes, they will enjoy safety too. Instead of plotting rebellion or wishing harm on their captors, they were to be peaceful and productive neighbors. God's people are called to bring good to the places where they live, even under rulers who do not know the Lord.

God warns the captives not to let local fortunetellers and pretended prophets trick them with promises of a quick return. The people liked hearing pleasant predictions, so they actively encouraged these dreamers to tell them flattering lies. The Lord declares firmly that He never sent these messengers and never spoke through them. We must test every spiritual claim by God's true word so we are not led astray by wishful thinking.

God sets a clear limit on the captivity, stating that it will last for seventy full years. Only after that whole period is finished will the Lord step in, fulfill His gracious promise, and bring them back to Judah. This specific timeframe was given to cure their impatience and stop them from acting ahead of God's schedule. God's promises never fail, but they arrive at His perfect time rather than ours.

The Lord assures His people that He knows His own purposes for them, and those purposes are for their good and peace rather than their destruction. His goal was not to wipe them out, but to give them a real future and a blessed hope. Even when God disciplines His people with hardship, His ultimate thoughts toward them are full of mercy. Trusting God's kind intentions gives believers quiet confidence during dark seasons.

differ.view: Believers can claim this promise through Christ, who secured all God's covenant blessings, but it points to ultimate spiritual salvation and eternal good rather than an earthly life free from trouble.
This promise was given specifically to ancient Jewish exiles under judgment, so individual Christians today should not lift it from its context as a guarantee of personal earthly success.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Many contemporary teachers use this verse to assure individual believers that God guarantees them personal health, wealth, and worldly success in this life.

notes.meaning: God promises that when the exile softens their hard hearts, the people will call on Him, and He will hear them. They will truly find Him whenever they seek Him with their whole heart instead of pretending. Affliction would finally cure their indifference and turn their casual prayers into sincere cries for mercy. God never turns away anyone who honestly seeks His face with an undivided heart.

The Lord declares that He will allow Himself to be found by His people and will end their long captivity. He will collect them from every nation and territory where they had been scattered and bring them back to Jerusalem. Even though the exiles seemed hopelessly separated, God had the power to gather them into one family again. No distance can keep God from rescuing those He has chosen to restore.

Some exiles brushed aside Jeremiah's words by claiming that God had already raised up true prophets for them right there in Babylon. These local leaders told the people what they wanted to hear about a fast rescue. God brings up their proud claim in order to show them how completely mistaken they were. It is dangerous to prefer cheerful lies over hard truths.

God answers those false hopes by describing what is in store for the king and the people still living back in Jerusalem. The exiles thought those left in the homeland were fortunate, but God says they will face war, starvation, and deadly plague. He compares those remaining residents to rotten, disgusting figs that are so foul they cannot be eaten. Outward privileges and staying in the holy city could not protect unrepentant sinners from judgment.

The Lord warns that He will chase down the survivors in Judah until other kingdoms look on them with horror, disgust, and mockery. This terrible ruin would fall on them because they continually ignored God's words sent through His prophets time after time. God notes that the captives in Babylon had shared that same stubborn habit of refusing to listen. Repeatedly ignoring God's warnings leaves a person without excuse when judgment arrives.

God calls every captive who was sent from Jerusalem to Babylon to listen carefully to His message. Even in a distant pagan country, they remained under the Lord's authority and needed His truth. Hearing God's voice was the only way they could avoid dangerous mistakes and find real peace. God never stops speaking truth to His people, even when they are under His discipline.

God names two specific deceivers in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, who told lies while pretending to speak for the Lord. The Lord announces that He will give them over to Nebuchadnezzar, who will execute them in front of the other exiles. Their political meddling and false promises would bring down the wrath of the Babylonian king upon their own heads. God often uses world leaders to expose and punish religious hypocrites.

The gruesome death of these two men would become a well-known curse phrase among the exiles in Babylon. When people wanted to curse someone, they would wish that the Lord make them like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom Nebuchadnezzar roasted alive in the fire. Burning was a common Babylonian punishment for stirring up unrest and rebellion. Those who lead others into rebellion against God's plans end up facing shameful disaster.

God lists the shameful crimes that brought this punishment: they committed adultery with their neighbors' wives and told unauthorized lies in God's name. They likely hid their secret sins from the public, but God declares that He saw everything and was an eyewitness against them. No sinner can hide behind a religious title when standing before the all-seeing Lord. Knowing that God sees all our private actions should lead us to walk in holiness.

God tells Jeremiah to deliver a judgment against Shemaiah, another deceptive leader living in Babylon. Shemaiah took it upon himself to send letters in his own name to the citizens of Jerusalem and to Zephaniah and the other priests. He acted with great arrogance, trying to direct temple affairs from hundreds of miles away without any divine calling. Taking religious authority into one's own hands without God's appointment leads to dangerous pride.

In his letter, Shemaiah told Zephaniah that God made him temple overseer to keep order and lock up any madman who claimed to be a prophet. He scolded Zephaniah for not silencing Jeremiah of Anathoth, who was telling the exiles to settle down for a long stay. Shemaiah twisted the idea of religious duty to demand that God's true prophet be thrown into iron collars and stocks. Wicked leaders often label God's faithful servants as crazy troublemakers to justify silencing them.

Zephaniah the priest took Shemaiah's threatening letter and read it directly to Jeremiah. Instead of locking the prophet up in the stocks, Zephaniah chose to let Jeremiah know what his enemies in Babylon were scheming. This gave Jeremiah the opportunity to hear the accusation and take the matter straight to God. The Lord often protects His messengers by giving them fair-minded listeners among community leaders.

God commands Jeremiah to send a message to all the exiles announcing the sentence against Shemaiah. Because Shemaiah prophesied without being sent and made the people trust in a lie, God would wipe out his family line entirely. Neither he nor any of his descendants would live to see the joyful restoration God had planned for His people. Teaching rebellion against God's truth brings lasting ruin on those who deceive others.
